They execute it on three IBM Quantum hardware systems and evaluate transpiled two-qubit gate count, total circuit depth, runtime, maximum absolute error (L-infinity norm), and root-mean-square error. They also introduce a sampler-based measurement strategy that reconstructs macroscopic density fields directly from computational-basis measurements instead of full quantum state tomography.
AI.result: The collision and streaming operators dominate overall cost and become the primary scalability bottleneck on current hardware. The sampler-based measurement approach substantially reduces measurement overhead while preserving the expected advection-diffusion dynamics on hardware. The abstract reports evaluation of gate count, depth, runtime, L-infinity error, and RMSE, but does not provide specific hardware device names or numerical metric values.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a quantitative assessment of QLBM performance in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum regime and identifies principal algorithmic and experimental limitations, especially the high cost of collision and streaming operators, that must be addressed before QLBM becomes viable for fluid dynamics.

title: Penetration of a sphere in a pool: Secondary pinch-off
summary:
The water entry of solid bodies, in particular spheres, has been the subject of numerous studies due to its relevance in multiple applications, especially focusing on cavity dynamics and the resulting forces and subsequent trajectories. The role of wettability in cavity formation and sustainability has been experimentally and theoretically addressed in the past; however, typically only up to the occurrence of a primary air cavity pinch-off. What is less explored is how wettability can influence higher-order pinch-offs. In the following study, especially secondary pinch-offs are shown to determine whether a sphere trajectory is terminally ascending, i.e., the sphere returns to the surface, or terminally descending: wettability is shown to be a strong influencing factor.
  This study begins with a series of systematic experiments, comparing the entry and trajectory of spheres over a range of impact Reynolds and Froude numbers, but also with varying surface wettability. From time resolved trajectories, a force balance is computed, illustrating the role of buoyancy, arising from the volume of any sustained air cavity in the wake of the sphere. Secondary pinch-offs alter this volume; hence, the terminal trajectory. A force-scale comparison and local radial balance at the cavity neck are then presented, suggesting how wettability influences the secondary pinch-off.

AI.tldr: An experimental study of sphere water entry shows that surface wettability influences secondary cavity pinch-off, which changes the volume of air retained in the sphere's wake, the buoyancy contribution to the force balance, and ultimately whether the sphere terminally returns to the surface or continues descending.
AI.motivation: Water entry of solid bodies such as spheres is important in many applications, and prior work has examined how wettability affects cavity formation and sustainability. However, existing studies typically consider only up to the primary air-cavity pinch-off, leaving higher-order pinch-offs—especially secondary pinch-offs—and their effect on terminal trajectory less explored.
AI.method: The study performs systematic sphere water-entry experiments over a range of impact Reynolds and Froude numbers and with varying surface wettability. Time-resolved trajectories are used to compute a force balance, including buoyancy arising from any sustained air cavity in the sphere's wake. A force-scale comparison and a local radial balance at the cavity neck are then used to suggest how wettability influences secondary pinch-off. Exact experimental ranges, materials, and quantitative force values are not provided in the abstract.
AI.result: Secondary pinch-offs are shown to alter the sustained air-cavity volume and therefore the terminal trajectory. Wettability is identified as a strong influencing factor determining whether the sphere's trajectory is terminally ascending, meaning it returns to the surface, or terminally descending. Quantitative trajectory or force results are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Wettability strongly influences higher-order cavity pinch-off during sphere water entry. By affecting secondary pinch-off and the associated retained air-cavity volume and buoyancy, wettability can determine the terminal trajectory of the sphere. The presented force-scale comparison and local radial balance at the cavity neck suggest a mechanism for this wettability effect.

title: The Generalized Twin Image: Understanding Regularized Phase Retrieval
summary: Image priors can dramatically improve phase retrieval reconstruction, but their effectiveness strongly varies between imaging modalities. We introduce the generalized twin image, which extends the classical twin-image ambiguity from Fourier phase retrieval to any invertible sensing operator, to understand this effectiveness. The ambiguity extends to undersampled and oversampled measurements, remaining exact under undersampling and for oversampled coded Fourier measurements. We show that it provides a simple criterion to assess regularization effectiveness: the image prior should favor the ground truth over its generalized twin image. We propose the total-variation ratio as a simple measure of this preference, and derive closed-form estimates for structured random phase retrieval models. Experiments with a pretrained denoiser demonstrate that the ratio predicts regularized reconstruction performance across different sensing models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the generalized twin image to explain why image priors vary in effectiveness for phase retrieval, proposes a total-variation ratio as a criterion for whether a prior favors the ground truth over its ambiguity, and shows experimentally that this ratio predicts regularized reconstruction performance across sensing models.
AI.motivation: Image priors can greatly improve phase retrieval, but their effectiveness depends strongly on the imaging modality. The authors aim to understand this variability and provide a principled criterion for assessing when regularization will be effective.
AI.method: The authors generalize the classical twin-image ambiguity from Fourier phase retrieval to any invertible sensing operator, analyze its behavior under undersampling and oversampling, and argue that an effective image prior should favor the ground truth over its generalized twin image. They propose the total-variation ratio as a simple measure of this preference and derive closed-form estimates for structured random phase retrieval models. They also conduct experiments using a pretrained denoiser.
AI.result: The generalized twin image remains exact under undersampling and for oversampled coded Fourier measurements. The proposed total-variation ratio is shown experimentally with a pretrained denoiser to predict regularized reconstruction performance across different sensing models. Specific datasets, numerical performance values, and detailed experimental metrics are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Regularization effectiveness in phase retrieval can be assessed by whether the image prior favors the ground truth over its generalized twin image. The total-variation ratio provides a simple such measure and can predict regularized reconstruction performance across sensing models.

title: Stabilization of counter propagating currents by energy conservation in collisions
summary: Current filamentation generates magnetic fields and shapes electron transport in dense plasmas, where collisions can either suppress or enhance its growth. Here we show that conserving electron kinetic energy in a collisional model can change both the dominant instability and its characteristic wavelength. We develop a linear kinetic theory for drifting, anisotropic electron populations with a relaxation operator that conserves particle number and laboratory-frame kinetic energy while allowing momentum transfer to a stationary ion background. For counterstreaming currents, energy conservation maintains the stabilizing influence of charge separation over a broader range of collision frequencies than a model conserving particle number alone. At intermediate collision rates, the resulting suppression of transverse filamentation allows a nearly aperiodic oblique mode to dominate, reducing the maximum growth rate and shifting the wavelength of the fastest-growing perturbation. Two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations support predicted growth rates of up to more than a magnitude lower than expected without energy conserving collision.

AI.tldr: An energy-conserving collisional model changes the dominant current-filamentation instability and its characteristic wavelength in dense plasmas; at intermediate collision rates, transverse filamentation is suppressed and a nearly aperiodic oblique mode dominates, with 2D PIC simulations supporting growth rates more than an order of magnitude lower than without energy-conserving collisions.
AI.motivation: Current filamentation generates magnetic fields and shapes electron transport in dense plasmas, and collisions can either suppress or enhance its growth. The paper addresses how conserving electron kinetic energy in a collisional model, rather than conserving particle number alone, affects the dominant instability and its characteristic wavelength.
AI.method: The authors develop a linear kinetic theory for drifting, anisotropic electron populations using a relaxation operator that conserves particle number and laboratory-frame kinetic energy while allowing momentum transfer to a stationary ion background. They analyze counterstreaming currents and compare energy-conserving collisions with a model conserving particle number alone, then use two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations to test the predicted growth rates.
AI.result: For counterstreaming currents, energy conservation maintains the stabilizing influence of charge separation over a broader range of collision frequencies than a particle-number-conserving model. At intermediate collision rates, suppression of transverse filamentation allows a nearly aperiodic oblique mode to dominate, reducing the maximum growth rate and shifting the wavelength of the fastest-growing perturbation. Two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations support predicted growth rates up to more than a magnitude lower than expected without energy-conserving collisions.
AI.conclusion: Conserving electron kinetic energy in the collisional model can change both the dominant instability and its characteristic wavelength. Energy-conserving collisions are important for accurately predicting current filamentation and associated growth rates in dense plasmas; models conserving particle number alone can overestimate filamentation growth.

title: A Hybrid Message-Passing and Electric-Field Representation for Electrostatic QM/MM Embedding with Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
summary: Within a hybrid quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics approach a small region of a large atomistic system is described quantum mechanically, while the rest of the system is represented by a classical force field. Despite this, the computational cost of the quantum calculation severely limits the accessible simulation and sampling time. Replacing the quantum calculation with a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) trained on quantum reference data can greatly increase the accessible simulation time. However, the accuracy and efficiency strongly depend on the specific way in which the MLIP incorporates information about the classical (electrostatic) environment. Here, we demonstrate that existing strategies based purely on features derived from an external electric field fail to distinguish certain environments, ultimately limiting their accuracy. As a solution, we propose an extension to the equivariant TensorNet architecture that mitigates this shortcoming by incorporating classical atoms close to the quantum region into the message-passing scheme, combined with features derived from the electric field for describing the environment farther away. We show that this combination achieves higher accuracy than either approach alone.

AI.tldr: Replacing quantum calculations in QM/MM with a machine learning interatomic potential can extend simulation time, but accuracy depends on how the classical electrostatic environment is represented. Field-only features fail to distinguish some environments; the proposed equivariant TensorNet extension includes nearby classical atoms in message passing and electric-field features for the distant environment, achieving higher accuracy than either approach alone.
AI.motivation: The computational cost of the quantum region severely limits QM/MM simulation and sampling time. MLIPs trained on quantum reference data can greatly increase accessible simulation time, but their accuracy and efficiency depend strongly on how the MLIP incorporates information about the classical electrostatic environment, and existing field-based strategies fail to distinguish certain environments.
AI.method: The authors propose an extension to the equivariant TensorNet architecture that incorporates classical atoms close to the quantum region into the message-passing scheme, combined with features derived from the external electric field to describe the environment farther away.
AI.result: Existing strategies based purely on features derived from an external electric field fail to distinguish certain environments, ultimately limiting their accuracy. The proposed combination achieves higher accuracy than either approach alone.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating nearby classical atoms into the equivariant TensorNet message-passing scheme alongside electric-field features for the more distant environment mitigates the shortcoming of field-only strategies and improves accuracy for MLIP-based QM/MM modeling. The abstract does not provide quantitative efficiency or accuracy results.

title: Viscoelastic behavior at high volume fraction of magnetorheological suspensions in the presence of discontinuous shear thickening
summary: This paper presents a study of the viscoelastic behavior of suspensions of carbonyl iron particles coated with a superplastifier molecule and dispersed in ethylene glycol. The experiments were done in plate-plate configuration with the rheometer MCR502 of Anton Paar. The discontinuous shear thickening (DST) transition manifests by a large jump of the storage and loss modulus. For low magnetic fields ( H <___50___kA/m) the increase of moduli is at least of two orders of magnitude compared to the one induced by the magnetic field in the absence of DST. The behavior of the critical strain and the critical stress where the transition happens are presented for different frequencies and fields and a qualitative interpretation of the observed behavior is presented.

AI.tldr: The paper studies viscoelasticity and discontinuous shear thickening (DST) in ethylene glycol suspensions of superplastifier-coated carbonyl iron particles, showing that DST causes large jumps in storage and loss moduli and strongly amplifies low-field magnetically induced moduli.
AI.motivation: The abstract does not explicitly state the motivation. It focuses on understanding the viscoelastic behavior and DST transition of magnetorheological suspensions under combined shear and magnetic fields.
AI.method: Suspensions of carbonyl iron particles coated with a superplastifier molecule and dispersed in ethylene glycol were tested in a plate-plate configuration using an Anton Paar MCR502 rheometer. Storage and loss moduli were measured, and the critical strain and critical stress of the DST transition were examined for different frequencies and magnetic fields.
AI.result: The DST transition appears as a large jump in storage and loss moduli. For low magnetic fields (H < 50 kA/m), the increase in moduli is at least two orders of magnitude greater than that induced by the magnetic field in the absence of DST. Critical strain and critical stress depend on frequency and field, and a qualitative interpretation is provided.
AI.conclusion: DST substantially amplifies the viscoelastic moduli of the studied suspension at low magnetic fields. The critical strain and stress characterizing the transition were mapped across frequencies and fields, with a qualitative interpretation offered.

title: Ultraviolet Raman spectroscopy using multimode aluminum oxide waveguides
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures; includes supplementary information (6 pages, 5 figures)
summary: Waveguide-based Raman spectroscopy offers a route toward compact and integrated photonic sensors. While most waveguide Raman platforms operate in the near-infrared, extending excitation toward the visible and ultraviolet is attractive because shorter excitation wavelengths can provide substantially stronger Raman scattering and access to resonance-enhanced molecular responses. This transition, however, places greater demands on the photonic material because of optical loss, absorption and waveguide-generated spectral background. Here, we investigate aluminum oxide ($Al_2O_3$) waveguides as a low-background platform for Raman spectroscopy at 532 nm and 325 nm using a back-collected excitation and detection geometry. At 532 nm, after normalization to the incident excitation power-time product, the measured $Al_2O_3$ background was more than two orders of magnitude lower than that of $Si_3N_4$. Under 325 nm excitation, the waveguides maintained a weak and reproducible spectral background across the investigated widths. Using immersion oil as a model analyte deposited over the waveguide surface, we demonstrate that analyte-specific Raman fingerprints can be recovered above the waveguide background at both wavelengths. Signal-to-background ratio and spectral contrast were used to quantify analyte visibility relative to the waveguide background, and both metrics consistently confirmed clear detection of the analyte bands. These results demonstrate that $Al_2O_3$ combines low measured spectral background with operation from the visible into the ultraviolet, providing a promising route toward integrated Raman spectroscopy at shorter excitation wavelengths.

AI.tldr: Aluminum oxide waveguides are evaluated as a low-background platform for visible and ultraviolet Raman spectroscopy, showing much lower background than Si3N4 at 532 nm and weak, reproducible background at 325 nm while enabling detection of analyte Raman fingerprints at both wavelengths.
AI.motivation: Compact integrated photonic Raman sensors are attractive, and shorter visible/ultraviolet excitation wavelengths can provide stronger Raman scattering and access resonance-enhanced molecular responses. However, moving beyond near-infrared excitation increases demands on photonic materials due to optical loss, absorption, and waveguide-generated spectral background.
AI.method: The authors investigated Al2O3 waveguides for Raman spectroscopy at 532 nm and 325 nm using a back-collected excitation and detection geometry. They compared the normalized Al2O3 background with that of Si3N4 at 532 nm, examined background behavior across waveguide widths at 325 nm, and used immersion oil as a model analyte deposited on the waveguide surface. Analyte visibility was quantified using signal-to-background ratio and spectral contrast.
AI.result: At 532 nm, the measured Al2O3 background normalized to the incident excitation power-time product was more than two orders of magnitude lower than that of Si3N4. At 325 nm, the waveguides showed a weak and reproducible spectral background across the investigated widths. Analyte-specific Raman fingerprints from immersion oil were recovered above the waveguide background at both wavelengths, and signal-to-background ratio and spectral contrast consistently confirmed clear detection of analyte bands.
AI.conclusion: Al2O3 combines low measured spectral background with operation from the visible into the ultraviolet, making it a promising platform for integrated Raman spectroscopy at shorter excitation wavelengths.

title: An approximate separation of the electron and positron degrees of freedom in the Dirac-Heisenberg-Wigner formalism
summary: Here we study the quantum relativistic phase-space description of the Dirac field referred to as the Dirac--Heisenberg--Wigner (DHW) formalism. By applying a systematic expansion procedure in weak electromagnetic fields (compared to the Schwinger critical field) and slow temporal and long spatial scales (compared to the Compton scales), the 16 scalar phase-space functions of the DHW equations can be reduced to 8 scalars. By making a further change of variables, the equations can be interpreted as four evolution equations for the electron degrees of freedom and four for the positron degrees of freedom. We refer to these equations as the weakly coupled electron-positron (WCEP) limit of the DHW equations. Unlike the case after a Foldy--Wouthuysen transformation has been made, the electron and positron degrees of freedom remain weakly coupled. Naturally, further approximations can be made on the 4+4 equations so that only 4 equations for one particle species remain. Importantly, the expansion scheme can be carried out to all orders, in which case the reduced 4+4 model, contrary to other reduced models, will cover most quantum relativistic effects. Specifically, this includes vacuum polarization, a phenomenon that otherwise has been added phenomenologically, but here appears naturally as a feature of the general expansion scheme.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the Dirac–Heisenberg–Wigner phase-space formalism and derives a weakly coupled electron–positron limit by expanding in weak electromagnetic fields and slow/long scales. The 16 scalar DHW functions reduce to 8, then to four electron and four positron equations; an all-orders version retains most quantum relativistic effects, including vacuum polarization.
AI.motivation: The abstract does not explicitly state the motivation. It indicates an aim to obtain a reduced phase-space description of the Dirac field and to show that an all-orders expansion can naturally incorporate quantum relativistic effects such as vacuum polarization.
AI.method: A systematic expansion is applied in weak electromagnetic fields relative to the Schwinger critical field and in slow temporal and long spatial scales relative to Compton scales. This reduces the 16 scalar phase-space functions of the DHW equations to 8. A further change of variables yields four evolution equations for electron degrees of freedom and four for positron degrees of freedom, termed the weakly coupled electron–positron (WCEP) limit. Further approximations can reduce this to four equations for one particle species, and the expansion can be carried out to all orders.
AI.result: In the WCEP limit, electron and positron degrees of freedom remain weakly coupled, unlike after a Foldy–Wouthuysen transformation. The reduced 4+4 model obtained from the all-orders expansion is stated to cover most quantum relativistic effects, specifically including vacuum polarization, which appears naturally as a feature of the expansion scheme rather than being added phenomenologically.
AI.conclusion: The DHW equations admit a systematic weak-field, slow/long-scale reduction to a weakly coupled 4+4 electron–positron model. Unlike other reduced models, its all-orders form can retain most quantum relativistic effects, including vacuum polarization, without phenomenological insertion. The abstract does not provide quantitative results or experimental validation.

title: FLUCS: a modular GPU-native framework for fluid and plasma turbulence
summary: We present FLUCS, an open-source framework for solving systems of partial differential equations efficiently on graphics processing units (GPUs), targeting models of fluid and plasma turbulence. It comprises a set of numerical solvers specialised for a well-defined class of problems and independently developed systems that supply specific systems of equations. This allows different models to share numerical infrastructure while retaining control over their individual implementation and optimisation. The present release provides a Fourier pseudospectral solver for one-, two-, and three-dimensional periodic domains solved on a single NVIDIA GPU, with integrating-factor time integration and several time-stepping and dealiasing methods. We verify its convergence, quantify its computational costs, and demonstrate its application to three reduced models of fusion and astrophysical plasma turbulence.

Its release includes a Fourier pseudospectral solver for 1D–3D periodic domains on a single NVIDIA GPU, with integrating-factor time integration and multiple time-stepping and dealiasing methods; convergence is verified, costs are quantified, and three reduced plasma turbulence models are demonstrated.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to enable efficient GPU-based solution of PDE systems for fluid and plasma turbulence while allowing different models to share numerical infrastructure without sacrificing control over their individual implementation and optimization.
AI.method: FLUCS combines numerical solvers specialized for a defined problem class with independently developed systems supplying specific equations. The present release provides a Fourier pseudospectral solver for one-, two-, and three-dimensional periodic domains on a single NVIDIA GPU, using integrating-factor time integration and several time-stepping and dealiasing methods. AI.conclusion: FLUCS provides open-source GPU numerical infrastructure for fluid and plasma turbulence PDE models, enabling shared numerical components while preserving model-specific implementation and optimization. title: Hydrodynamic regimes of the edge-tone in a simplified recorder mouthpiece
summary: The acoustic mechanism of flue instruments originates in the interaction of an air jet with a sharp edge, the labium. Previous studies have examined isolated edge-tones or full instruments in which acoustic resonance obscures the underlying hydrodynamics, and a systematic understanding of how geometric parameters govern jet stability is lacking. We present a large-scale parametric study of the jet-labium interaction in a simplified recorder mouthpiece without a resonator, using more than 200 two-dimensional direct numerical simulations with an immersed boundary method. We vary the mouth distance, the labium angle, the vertical offset of the labium, and the Reynolds number (Re), and characterize the dynamics through spectra of the transverse force on the labium. The baseline configuration oscillates as a predominantly periodic Stage I edge-tone with Strouhal number St ~ 0.07, nearly constant for Re >= 330 and for all labium angles at the baseline mouth distance, so the frequency is set by the geometry rather than by viscosity. The mouth distance has the strongest influence: it is the only parameter that introduces a second oscillation stage, and the Stage I frequency is inversely proportional to it. The second stage is weakly present at five and six windway heights, established from six and a half, and dominant from eight, where it strongly modulates the amplitude. The vertical offset mainly affects the strength of the oscillation, and the labium angle does not change the instability mechanism. A baseline configuration is identified for future aeroacoustic coupling studies.

AI.tldr: A parametric 2D DNS study of jet-labium interaction in a resonator-free simplified recorder mouthpiece shows that mouth distance is the dominant geometric control on edge-tone stages, while Reynolds number, vertical offset, and labium angle have weaker or more limited effects.

AI.method: The authors performed more than 200 two-dimensional direct numerical simulations using an immersed boundary method for a simplified recorder mouthpiece without a resonator. They varied mouth distance, labium angle, labium vertical offset, and Reynolds number, and characterized the dynamics using spectra of the transverse force on the labium.

title: Reconfigurable Generation of Terahertz Spiral Vector Beams Based on All-Dielectric Cascaded Metasurfaces
summary: The reconfigurable generation of complex structured terahertz (THz) fields, and vector beams in particular, remains a significant challenge. Here, we propose a novel all-dielectric cascaded-metasurface scheme for the reconfigurable generation of THz spiral vector beams. By combining an isotropic phase-compensation layer with an anisotropic circular-polarization-sensitive layer, together with a new phase design tailored to spiral beams, we achieve independent control of the left- and right-handed circularly polarized (LCP and RCP) components through the relative rotation angle between the two layers. Under linearly polarized THz wave illumination, THz vector beams with switchable spiral numbers of 1-3 and reversible circular-polarization handedness are demonstrated at frequencies around 0.9 THz. Moreover, owing to the longitudinal evolution characteristic of spiral beams, the three generated THz vector beams exhibit azimuthal rotations of 279.9°, 125.7° and 75.5°, respectively, along the propagation direction. Such complex THz vector beams, which combine reconfigurability with longitudinal evolution, are expected to find applications in emerging fields such as next-generation wireless communications and THz imaging. The proposed generation scheme also offers a useful reference for the reconfigurable generation of high-dimensional vector beams.

AI.motivation: Reconfigurable generation of complex structured terahertz fields, especially vector beams, remains a significant challenge.
AI.method: An all-dielectric cascaded metasurface combines an isotropic phase-compensation layer with an anisotropic circular-polarization-sensitive layer and a new phase design tailored to spiral beams. The relative rotation angle between the two layers independently controls the LCP and RCP components under linearly polarized THz illumination.

title: Accelerating Computation and Resolving Extraneous Roots in the Kinetic Plasma Dispersion Relation Solver BO
comment: 21 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Code available at https://github.com/FusionAlpha/botian
summary: Kinetic dispersion relations are widely used to study waves and instabilities in space, astrophysical, and laboratory plasmas. Iterative root searches depend on initial guesses and may fail to converge or miss important branches. The BO/PDRK solvers [Comput. Phys. Commun. 244, 343-371 (2019)] use rational pole expansions to transform the nonlinear dispersion relation into a matrix eigenvalue problem, obtaining all roots of the approximated relation in one calculation. However, high cyclotron harmonics enlarge the matrix and slow computation, while extraneous roots are difficult to separate from physical modes. We develop BO-T (BO-Tian), an improved version of BO combining two methods. First, for matrix reduction, BO-T applies rank factorization to combined residue matrices, preserving the rational dispersion relation and accounting for the removed pole eigenvalues. Second, for root screening, BO-T uses contour comparison between approximate and reference kinetic dispersion matrices along a closed contour enclosing no poles. This provides a sufficient condition for preserving local root counts, with error bounds for isolated roots and criteria for growth rate signs. Benchmarks on representative electrostatic and electromagnetic cases show speedups of about 10 to 140 for matrix assembly and eigenvalue calculation, exceeding 30 in most cases with high cyclotron harmonics. Root screening recovers the main unstable branches in agreement with published and archived dispersion curves.

title: ART of PIV: Agentic Real-Time Particle Image Velocimetry for Active Flow Control
summary: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) measures fluid motion from images of tracer particles, but its accuracy depends on choices throughout the estimation pipeline, including image preprocessing, flow estimation, and postprocessing. These choices are typically left to expert tuning, and a fixed configuration can become less accurate as conditions change. This matters especially when PIV supplies feedback for real-time control, where measurements must be both accurate and fast, and flow conditions vary. We introduce ART of PIV -- short for Agentic Real-Time and also a nod to the art of tuning a PIV pipeline -- which automates pipeline choice for each image pair. A learned agent selects a configuration according to a chosen measurement objective from a library assembled for a specified speed budget. Across cross-correlation, classical optical-flow, and learning-based estimators, ART of PIV reduces average end-point error (AEPE) by 12.2-22.4 % relative to the best single estimator at matched speed, with gains extending to 1000-4000 image pair/s. In a simulated local velocity regulation task, it reduces mean normalized closed-loop cost by 13.24-13.59 percentage points relative to a tuned fixed estimator, with the same classical controller in both cases. In a tabletop water channel, we illustrate two ways to tune ART of PIV for a fluidic pinball of three rotating cylinders: selecting between complementary optical-flow tunings for accuracy, and selecting regions of interest with coherent rotation or shear using a common flow estimator. For the first variant, we train a DreamerV3 reinforcement learning controller directly in the physical world and demonstrate tracking of a prescribed flow field in the wake of a fluidic pinball.

title: Non-Hermitian Spectral Topology Shaped by Memory
summary: Non-Hermitian spectral topology has transformed our understanding of bulk--boundary correspondence in open systems, yet its exploration has largely remained within the Markovian regime of instantaneous coupling. Here, we reveal how memory shapes non-Hermitian spectral topology by extending coupling asymmetry from space to time. Spatiotemporal nonreciprocity and memory-induced spectral multivaluedness give rise to nontrivial spectral topology on multi-sheeted Riemann surfaces, governed by both spatial connectivity and interaction history. Coherent interference among long-range memory channels can induce anomalous spectral winding and skin localization opposite to the dominant-coupling direction. Moreover, asymmetric retardation alone can generate non-Hermitian spectral topology and skin accumulation even in the absence of spatial coupling asymmetry. Channel dissipation further drives topological transitions that reverse the skin effect, with a critical point at matched channel and lattice decay rates. We validate the anomalous skin effect and its dissipation-controlled reversal through full-wave simulations and microwave experiments. Our results establish time nonlocality as a fundamental degree of freedom in non-Hermitian topology, revealing phenomena inaccessible within the Markovian paradigm.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that temporal memory and spatiotemporal nonreciprocity extend non-Hermitian spectral topology beyond the Markovian regime, producing multivalued Riemann-surface spectra, anomalous and reversed skin effects, and dissipation-driven topological transitions, validated by full-wave simulations and microwave experiments.
AI.motivation: Non-Hermitian spectral topology and bulk-boundary correspondence in open systems have been studied mainly under Markovian instantaneous coupling; the paper aims to reveal how memory and time nonlocality reshape this topology.

title: Plasmoid Instability in Inhomogeneous Current Sheets
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures, submitted to Plasma and Fusion Research
summary: Plasmoid instability in inhomogeneous current sheets is investigated using electromagnetic gyrokinetic simulations of collisionless magnetic reconnection. Simulations with and without small random perturbations are compared to examine the effects of symmetry breaking and spatial inhomogeneity. The current-sheet width immediately before disruption remains close to the electron skin depth, whereas the disruption aspect ratio varies significantly between primary and later current sheets. Random perturbations also produce asymmetric plasmoid topologies in which neighboring X points no longer share a common separatrix. These results suggest that spatial inhomogeneity is an important factor in the disruption of dynamically evolving current sheets.

AI.tldr: Electromagnetic gyrokinetic simulations of collisionless reconnection show that inhomogeneous current sheets disrupt with widths near the electron skin depth, while disruption aspect ratios and plasmoid topologies vary; spatial inhomogeneity is suggested to be important in current-sheet disruption.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates plasmoid instability in inhomogeneous current sheets and examines the effects of symmetry breaking and spatial inhomogeneity by comparing simulations with and without small random perturbations.
AI.method: The study uses electromagnetic gyrokinetic simulations of collisionless magnetic reconnection, comparing simulations with and without small random perturbations.

title: A Large Eddy Simulation Study of Turbine Pitch Motion Effects on Power Generation in Fully Developed Floating Wind Turbine Arrays
summary: Interactions between floating wind turbines and the marine atmospheric boundary layer affect turbine wakes and power output. This study examines the impact of turbine representations and platform pitching motion on power predictions for aligned floating wind turbine arrays. Large-eddy simulations (LES) are performed for a fully developed wind turbine array boundary layer with periodic streamwise and spanwise boundary conditions and moving surface drag (MOSD) at the bottom surface. A proposed power-curve-aware extension of the conventional actuator disk model (PCADM) is compared with the traditional constant coefficient actuator disk model (CCADM), which is valid in principle only during Region 2 operation. Harmonic pitching motion matched to a representative ocean wave frequency is prescribed for IEA 15MW turbines mounted on the UMaine VolturnUS-S platform. Results demonstrate that the CCADM produces unphysical power overshoot when relative velocities induced by harmonic pitching periodically exceed rated speed, while the PCADM eliminates these unrealistic excursions from the actual turbine operating range. Various wind-wave conditions and relative pitching motions for an aligned farm with PCADM turbines are analyzed, including in-phase, opposite-phase, and incommensurate-phase row-to-row relative turbine motion. Results reveal that, depending on operational regions, turbine pitching motion can either increase or decrease mean turbine power output. Among the relative phases considered, in-phase motions produce larger fluctuations at the farm scale due to stronger turbine-turbine correlations. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for turbine motion and associated changes in operational regions when modeling turbine and wind farm power production in LES of offshore floating wind farms using actuator disk representations.

AI.tldr: This study uses large-eddy simulations to assess how actuator-disk turbine representations and platform pitching affect power predictions for aligned floating wind turbine arrays. A power-curve-aware actuator disk model avoids unphysical overshoot from the conventional constant-coefficient model and captures phase-dependent changes in mean power and farm-scale fluctuations.
AI.motivation: Interactions between floating wind turbines and the marine atmospheric boundary layer affect turbine wakes and power output. The conventional constant-coefficient actuator disk model is valid in principle only during Region 2 operation, so turbine motion and associated changes in operational regions need to be accounted for when modeling floating offshore wind farms in large-eddy simulations.

title: Dual-rate optical frequency comb based on a cylindrical microresonator with a nanoscale radius variation
summary: We theoretically find that a cylindrical microresonator with nanoscale radius variation can be a source of coherent microcombs with two repetition rates, independently controlled by the device geometry. This phenomenon arises from the formation of two-dimensional axial-azimuthal dissipative Kerr solitons (2D DKS), which we discovered through numerical simulations of the nonlinearly coupled Lugiato-Lefever equations with realistic microresonator device parameters. We demonstrate that, despite the variation in the dispersion characteristics of azimuthal modes at different axial numbers, the spontaneous synchronization mechanism leads to a unified soliton repetition rate. We consider near-parabolic variations in the radius of a cylindrical resonator, compatible with the surface nanoscale axial photonics (SNAP) platform. In our example, we generate 2D DKS with an azimuthal rate of approximately 329 GHz and an axial rate of 6 GHz, which can be adjusted on demand by selecting the appropriate resonator geometry, thereby promising compact sources of frequency combs operating simultaneously across different frequency scales.

AI.tldr: The paper theoretically and numerically shows that a cylindrical microresonator with nanoscale, near-parabolic radius variation can support two-dimensional axial-azimuthal dissipative Kerr solitons, enabling coherent microcombs with two geometry-controlled repetition rates. An example yields approximately 329 GHz azimuthal and 6 GHz axial rates.
AI.motivation: The work aims to realize compact coherent frequency-comb sources that can operate simultaneously across different frequency scales by generating microcombs with two independently controllable repetition rates from a single device.
AI.method: The authors perform numerical simulations of nonlinearly coupled Lugiato-Lefever equations using realistic microresonator parameters. They consider a cylindrical microresonator with nanoscale radius variation compatible with the surface nanoscale axial photonics (SNAP) platform and analyze two-dimensional axial-azimuthal dissipative Kerr solitons, including spontaneous synchronization of soliton repetition rates despite axial-number-dependent azimuthal dispersion.
AI.result: Two-dimensional dissipative Kerr solitons are predicted, with an azimuthal repetition rate of approximately 329 GHz and an axial repetition rate of 6 GHz in the presented example. The rates can be adjusted on demand by selecting the resonator geometry, and spontaneous synchronization leads to a unified soliton repetition rate despite variation in azimuthal-mode dispersion across axial numbers.
AI.conclusion: A cylindrical microresonator with nanoscale radius variation can serve as a source of coherent microcombs with two repetition rates independently controlled by device geometry, promising compact frequency-comb sources operating simultaneously across different frequency scales. title: Teacher-guided multi-task learning for integrated plasma monitoring on EAST
summary: This paper integrates tokamak plasma disruption prediction, Edge-Localized Mode (ELM) monitoring, Multifaceted Asymmetric Radiation From the Edge (MARFE) detection, and H/L-mode identification into a unified Multi-Task Learning (MTL) model. This integration aims to realize MTL's potential for improving task performance while reducing inference time. However, on datasets constructed from selected EAST discharges recorded between 2015 and 2020, this study found that the traditional MTL method underperformed the corresponding Single-Task Learning (STL) method on some tasks. This performance degradation is the well-known issue of negative transfer. To address this issue, this study proposes the teacher-guided MTL method, using task-specific STL ensembles (teachers) to guide the training of an MTL model (student). The ensemble teachers guide training through soft-target distillation losses for each task of the MTL student model, and increased weighting of each shot's peak-disruptivity window in the disruption prediction label-supervised loss. Test-set results showed that the teacher-guided MTL method outperformed the corresponding STL method in ROC-AUC for all four tasks, eliminating the negative transfer observed with the traditional MTL method. In addition, on the same single GPU or single physical CPU core, the MTL student model can substantially reduce the inference time required to generate all four task outputs compared with the four STL baseline models. This paper offers a promising route to plasma monitoring systems that cover a broader range of phenomena, improve per-task performance and reduce inference time with limited real-time computational resources, supporting future high-performance plasma operation.

AI.tldr: The paper unifies EAST tokamak disruption prediction, ELM monitoring, MARFE detection, and H/L-mode identification in a multi-task learning model; because conventional MTL showed negative transfer on 2015–2020 EAST data, it proposes teacher-guided MTL using task-specific STL ensembles, which improved ROC-AUC for all four tasks over STL and reduced inference time versus four STL models.
AI.motivation: The study aims to integrate four plasma-monitoring tasks into a unified multi-task learning model to improve task performance and reduce inference time, while addressing the negative transfer observed when conventional MTL underperformed single-task learning on some tasks.
AI.method: Using datasets from selected EAST discharges recorded between 2015 and 2020, the study compares conventional MTL with STL and proposes teacher-guided MTL, in which task-specific STL ensembles act as teachers for an MTL student. AI.conclusion: Teacher-guided MTL offers a promising route for plasma monitoring systems that cover more phenomena, improve per-task performance, and reduce inference time under limited real-time computational resources, supporting future high-performance plasma operation.

title: An analytical framework for wave-coherent airflow over fast surface waves
summary: Classical theories attribute wind-wave momentum transfer to a critical layer, where the mean wind speed equals the wave phase speed. For waves that travel faster than the near-surface wind, this layer may lie outside the wave boundary layer or be absent altogether. We develop an analytical description of the wave-coherent airflow in this regime for a prescribed mean wind, using a Wentzel--Kramers--Brillouin--Jeffreys (WKBJ) approximation to the viscous Orr--Sommerfeld equation in wave-following coordinates. The solution combines an outer Rayleigh mode, which carries the dominant wave-coherent motion, with a thin viscous Stokes layer that supplies the phase shift producing the pressure form stress. At leading order, the form stress scales with the inverse square root of the wave Reynolds number, with a coefficient set by an integral of the outer response, and transfers momentum from the waves to the air. For an exponential mean profile, the WKBJ approximation gives closed-form expressions for the wave-coherent response. To accommodate the rapid near-surface variation of realistic wall-bounded profiles, we develop a long-wave expansion near the surface and match it to the outer WKBJ mode (LW--WKBJ). For wall-modelled simulations, whose first resolved level lies above the viscous sublayer, we replace the molecular viscosity in the Stokes layer with a constant-stress effective viscosity. Using mean profiles from direct numerical simulations and wave-phase-resolved large-eddy simulations, the LW--WKBJ framework closely reproduces the dominant wave-coherent velocity and pressure obtained from numerical solutions and available simulation data. The predicted form-stress coefficients also agree well with the available LES estimates.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a WKBJ-based analytical framework, including an LW-WKBJ extension, to describe wave-coherent airflow and form stress when waves travel faster than the near-surface wind; it predicts inverse-square-root wave-Reynolds-number scaling and agrees with DNS/LES data.
AI.motivation: Classical wind-wave momentum-transfer theories rely on a critical layer where mean wind speed equals wave phase speed. For waves faster than the near-surface wind, this layer may be outside the wave boundary layer or absent, so an analytical description of the wave-coherent airflow in this regime is needed.
AI.method: The authors use a WKBJ approximation to the viscous Orr-Sommerfeld equation in wave-following coordinates for a prescribed mean wind. The solution combines an outer Rayleigh mode carrying dominant wave-coherent motion with a thin viscous Stokes layer producing the phase shift and pressure form stress. At leading order, form stress scales with the inverse square root of the wave Reynolds number, with a coefficient set by an integral of the outer response, and transfers momentum from waves to air. A long-wave near-surface expansion matched to the outer WKBJ mode gives the LW-WKBJ framework for realistic wall-bounded profiles. For wall-modelled simulations, molecular viscosity in the Stokes layer is replaced by a constant-stress effective viscosity.

Predicted form-stress coefficients also agree well with available LES estimates.
AI.conclusion: The proposed WKBJ and LW-WKBJ framework provides an analytical description of wave-coherent airflow and form stress for waves faster than the near-surface wind, including wall-modelled simulation conditions, and is validated against available DNS and LES results.

title: Non-contact temperature sensing and optical scatter in cryogenically-cooled crystalline silicon
summary: Cryogenic crystalline silicon is a promising optical material for next generation gravitational-wave detectors due to its low mechanical loss (a driver of thermal noise), high thermal conductivity and zero coefficient of thermal expansion at 123 K. In this paper, we report on the design and results of an experiment to measure the temperature of a flat-flat uncoated crystalline silicon sample using a non-contact sensing method relying on interference (optical fringes) made from reflections between the front and back surfaces. We also propose a scheme for implementation of this technique for cryogenic test masses in future gravitational-wave detectors such as Einstein Telescope and LIGO Voyager. Additionally, we characterize the optical scattering of the sample in vacuum at cryogenic temperatures by using a high-sensitivity infrared camera. We measured relatively constant scatter with an average bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) of $(4.43\pm0.2)\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{sr^{-1}}$ at a scattering angle of $θ_{s} = 7.5^\circ$ over the (cold-plate) temperature range of 123-294 K and saw no evidence for growth of cryogenic molecular layers (ice) on the sample in our current setup.

AI.tldr: The paper reports a non-contact optical-fringe method to measure the temperature of a flat-flat uncoated crystalline silicon sample, proposes its use for cryogenic test masses in future gravitational-wave detectors, and characterizes cryogenic optical scattering, finding an average BRDF of (4.43±0.2)×10^-3 sr^-1 at 7.5° over 123–294 K with no observed ice-layer growth in the current setup.
AI.motivation: Cryogenic crystalline silicon is a promising optical material for next-generation gravitational-wave detectors because of its low mechanical loss, which drives thermal noise, high thermal conductivity, and zero coefficient of thermal expansion at 123 K. The work addresses the need for non-contact temperature sensing and characterization of optical scattering for cryogenic test masses.
AI.method: The authors designed and performed an experiment to measure the temperature of a flat-flat uncoated crystalline silicon sample using a non-contact sensing method based on interference optical fringes formed by reflections between the front and back surfaces. They also propose a scheme to implement this technique for cryogenic test masses in future detectors such as Einstein Telescope and LIGO Voyager, and characterize the sample’s optical scattering in vacuum at cryogenic temperatures using a high-sensitivity infrared camera.
AI.result: The measured scatter was relatively constant, with an average bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) of (4.43±0.2)×10^-3 sr^-1 at a scattering angle of θs = 7.5° over the cold-plate temperature range of 123–294 K. title: Equipartition between Alfvénic turbulence and energetic ions as the origin of the -5 common spectrum in the heliosphere
summary: Suprathermal ion tails throughout the heliosphere follow a ``common spectrum,'' $f(v)\propto v^{-5}$. We show that scale-by-scale equipartition between strong Alfvénic turbulence and the ions it accelerates predicts both this exponent and the absolute amplitude, $F(v)=B^2/(16π^3 m_i v^5)$, with no free parameters. The prediction agrees within a factor of a few with ACE and Voyager 1 spectra across three decades in magnetic energy. We argue that this saturated level is reached where strong turbulence accelerates particles locally; quiet-time tails lie well below it, consistent with nonlocal acceleration.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that scale-by-scale equipartition between strong Alfvénic turbulence and the suprathermal ions it accelerates explains the observed common ion-tail spectrum f(v) ∝ v^-5 and its absolute amplitude without free parameters, with agreement against ACE and Voyager 1 data.
AI.motivation: Suprathermal ion tails across the heliosphere exhibit a common spectrum, f(v) ∝ v^-5; the work aims to explain both this exponent and the absolute spectral amplitude from turbulence-particle energy balance.
AI.method: The authors derive a parameter-free prediction by assuming scale-by-scale equipartition between strong Alfvénic turbulence and the ions it accelerates, yielding F(v)=B^2/(16π^3 m_i v^5), and compare this prediction with ACE and Voyager 1 spectra.
AI.result: The equipartition argument predicts both the v^-5 exponent and the absolute amplitude, agreeing within a factor of a few with ACE and Voyager 1 spectra across three decades in magnetic energy. The saturated level is interpreted as occurring where strong turbulence accelerates particles locally; quiet-time tails are well below it, consistent with nonlocal acceleration.
AI.conclusion: A saturated equipartition level between strong Alfvénic turbulence and accelerated ions can account for the common suprathermal ion-tail spectrum and amplitude without free parameters; local versus nonlocal acceleration may explain whether tails reach this level. Specific fit metrics and additional datasets are not provided in the abstract.

title: Microswimmers lose by swimming selfishly
summary: At low Reynolds number, microswimmers are coupled by the flows they create, even when they are apart. The best way for each swimmer to push itself forward then depends on its neighbors, turning swimming together into a game. To study this, we optimize the shape changes of soft swimmers, alone and in pairs, with a differentiable Stokes solver. From random initial membrane motions, a lone swimmer converges to a traveling membrane wave. In a pair, the stroke of a swimmer affects its neighbor far more than the neighbor affects its own best stroke. For swimmers in line, this influence decays as $1/\ell$ with their separation $\ell$, whereas the incentive to respond decays as $1/\ell^2$. Selfish swimmers, which maximize their own payoff, respond only to the weak incentive. The cooperative gain they miss decays only as $1/\ell^2$, and their selfish adaptations leave the pair worse off than if both had kept their solitary strokes. Related swimmers, which also value the payoff of their neighbor, recover this gain, whereas competitors pay to hinder each other, both following a law that we derive analytically. Hydrodynamics alone thus makes swimming in company a social dilemma, whose outcome depends on how much the swimmers value each other.

AI.tldr: The paper models low-Reynolds-number microswimmers as soft bodies whose shape changes are optimized with a differentiable Stokes solver, alone and in pairs. A lone swimmer learns a traveling membrane wave; paired swimmers face a hydrodynamic game in which neighbor effects and incentives decay with separation, and selfish optimization can make both worse off than maintaining solitary strokes.
AI.motivation: At low Reynolds number, microswimmers are coupled by the flows they create even when separated, so each swimmer's best propulsive strategy depends on its neighbors; this turns swimming together into a game that the paper aims to study.
AI.method: The authors optimize the shape changes of soft swimmers, both alone and in pairs, using a differentiable Stokes solver, starting from random initial membrane motions. They analyze pairwise hydrodynamic interactions, including swimmers in line, and derive analytically a law governing related and competing swimmers.
AI.result: A lone swimmer converges from random initial membrane motions to a traveling membrane wave. In a pair, a swimmer's stroke affects its neighbor much more than the neighbor affects its own best stroke. For swimmers in line, this influence decays as 1/l with separation l, while the incentive to respond decays as 1/l^2. Selfish swimmers, maximizing their own payoff, respond only to the weak incentive; the cooperative gain they miss decays only as 1/l^2, and their selfish adaptations leave the pair worse off than if both had kept their solitary strokes. Related swimmers, which also value the neighbor's payoff, recover this gain, whereas competitors pay to hinder each other, both following the analytically derived law.
AI.conclusion: Hydrodynamics alone makes swimming in company a social dilemma, and the outcome depends on how much the swimmers value each other's payoff.

title: Intensity-Domain Demultiplexing of Orbital Angular Momentum Channels for Optical Communication
summary: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) multiplexing has been limited in practice by the complexity and optical loss of the elements that separate the channels at the receiver side. Here we adopt the azimuthal harmonics of OAM petal patterns as the demultiplexing basis, which makes the receiver the optical counterpart of the circular antenna arrays used in radio OAM links: the petal pattern of topological charge $\ell$ carries a single azimuthal harmonic of order $2\ell$, so one Fourier transform of the azimuthal intensity profile returns every channel, without gratings or mode sorters. The petals are formed by projecting a vector vortex beam from a single q-plate onto a linear polarization. A two-channel system at 515 nm with a 16-position circular photoreceiver array reaches 5.2 Gb/s below the forward error correction threshold, 2.6 Gb/s per channel from a 1.4 GHz photoreceiver.

AI.tldr: A two-channel OAM link uses the azimuthal harmonics of OAM petal patterns as a demultiplexing basis, avoiding gratings and mode sorters and achieving 5.2 Gb/s at 515 nm.
AI.motivation: OAM multiplexing has been limited in practice by the complexity and optical loss of the elements used to separate channels at the receiver.
AI.method: The authors use azimuthal harmonics of OAM petal patterns as the demultiplexing basis: a petal pattern with topological charge ℓ carries a single azimuthal harmonic of order 2ℓ, so one Fourier transform of the azimuthal intensity profile returns every channel without gratings or mode sorters. Petals are formed by projecting a vector vortex beam from a single q-plate onto a linear polarization.
